extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors, patent attorneys, inventors, and claim drafters seeking practical advice on strengthening patent claims
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on how to draft patent claims that are both defensible against validity attacks and valuable for enforcement/commercial coverage. Focuses on claim structure, specification support, infringement detectability, and portfolio prosecution practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong Claims Have Two Properties
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) They survive validity attacks (no anticipation, not obvious, definite, enabled, supported by written description). (2) They cover commercially valuable activity (the kinds of products competitors actually want to make).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim must satisfy patentability/validity requirements and also read on economically important competitor activity; both aspects are necessary for a "strong" claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element Count - Fewer Is Generally Better
rubrics_metrics.description: Each element is a hurdle the patentee must clear in proving infringement, and each is a target for invalidity attack. A claim with 5 elements is generally stronger than the same invention claimed with 12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize the number of elements where possible to reduce infringement proof burden and avenues for attack, but do not delete elements required to distinguish the prior art—those must remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Numerical Limits Unless They Distinguish
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wherein the temperature is between 50 and 100 degrees Celsius" is a hard limit. If the prior art discloses 49 or 101, the limit was needed; if not, the limit was unnecessary scope-shrinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only add numeric ranges/limits when they are necessary to overcome prior art; otherwise they unnecessarily narrow claim scope and weaken the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional Language - Useful but Risky
rubrics_metrics.description: "A processor configured to determine X" is functionally claimed. It is broader (covers any processor that determines X) but invokes 112(f) under Williamson if there is not enough surrounding structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claim language can broaden scope but risks being limited to disclosed structure under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (per Williamson); pair functional language with concrete structural elements to reduce 112 risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong Spec Support for Each Element
rubrics_metrics.description: Every claim element should have at least one paragraph of spec discussion explaining what it is, what it does, what alternatives exist, and how it interacts with neighboring elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide robust specification disclosure for each claim element—sparse support creates a §112 vulnerability (written description/enablement issues). Explain purpose, alternatives, and interactions in the spec.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detectability of Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that requires inspecting the source code of a competitor's product is hard to enforce - you cannot get discovery without filing suit, and you cannot file suit without a Rule 11 basis to believe infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to read on observable behaviors (network packets, UI flows, product packaging, physical outputs) whenever practicable, because such claims are easier to investigate and enforce than claims requiring opaque internal inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-Actor Drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Method claims should describe a single entity performing every step. After Akamai v. Limelight (Fed. Cir. 2015), divided infringement requires either a directing/controlling relationship or joint enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer single-actor claim formulations to avoid divided-infringement issues; if multi-actor steps are necessary, draft to capture directing/controlling relationships or joint-enterprise circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust to Construction Variation
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest claims read on the accused product under both broad and narrow constructions of the disputed terms. If your infringement read depends on a single favorable claim construction, you are betting the case on one issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to draft claims that will cover the target product across plausible claim constructions—avoid reliance on a single, optimistic construction for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Differentiation Within Family
rubrics_metrics.description: Different claims in the same patent should differ on legally meaningful dimensions - different scope, different element types, different transitions - not trivial restatements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dependent and alternative claims to cover materially different scope or embodiments; avoid wasted dependent claims that merely restate the independent claim without adding legal distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation Discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the strongest claim does not future-proof a portfolio. Always have a continuation pending so new claims can be drafted as new infringers emerge or as new claim-construction trends develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain continuations to adapt claim scope over time—file follow-on applications to pursue changed enforcement or claim-construction landscapes and to capture newly relevant competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Counterparts Strengthen Validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent that has been independently granted in EPO, JPO, and CNIPA is harder to invalidate in the US. The independent grants are evidence of patentability strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution successes and independent grants in major foreign jurisdictions can serve as persuasive evidence of patentability in US litigation/invalidity contexts; pursue international prosecution strategically to bolster overall portfolio strength.
